# Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect and Client VPN: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=hybrid-networking-q006 -->
### Question 1

A company has one AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection at a location in the United States. A private virtual interface on the connection is attached to the virtual private gateway of a VPC in us-east-1. The company adds a VPC in eu-west-1, a second Region, and that VPC must reach the data center privately over the same connection. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a second private virtual interface on the connection, and attach it directly to the virtual private gateway of the VPC in eu-west-1.
- Create a public virtual interface on the connection, and use it to reach the private IP addresses of the VPC in eu-west-1.
- Create a Direct Connect gateway, attach a new private virtual interface to it, and associate the virtual private gateways of both VPCs with it.
- Create a transit gateway in each Region, attach each VPC to the transit gateway in its Region, and connect both through a transit virtual interface.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Direct Connect gateway, attach a new private virtual interface to it, and associate the virtual private gateways of both VPCs with it.

**Deciding phrases.** "a second Region", "privately over the same connection", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: one existing connection in the United States, a new VPC in eu-west-1, private access, and the same connection.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a Direct Connect gateway, because it is a global resource that lets one private virtual interface reach VPCs in other Regions.
4. I remove the public virtual interface, because it reaches public services, not the private addresses of a VPC. I remove the direct attachment in eu-west-1, because a private virtual interface without a gateway reaches the associated Region only.
5. Between the Direct Connect gateway and the two transit gateways the difference is what the team must run; the stem asks for the LEAST operational overhead, so the transit gateways add work without a feature that the stem needs.
6. Check: the Direct Connect gateway uses the same connection, stays private, and reaches both Regions. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The deciding phrases are a second Region and the same connection. A Direct Connect gateway is [a globally available resource](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-dxgw-global-resource-any-region-not-china), and with it you reach [any AWS Region](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-dxgw-any-region-from-any-location) from a Direct Connect location. Associating both virtual private gateways with it is the smallest change.

**Why not.**

- "Create a second private virtual interface on the ...": Attached directly, a private virtual interface [reaches a VPC in the associated Region only](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-private-vif-without-dxgw-reaches-associated-region-only), and this connection is in the United States.
- "Create a public virtual interface on the connection, ...": A public virtual interface [enables access to public services](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vif-public-vs-private) such as Amazon S3; a private virtual interface [enables access to your VPC](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vif-public-vs-private).
- "Create a transit gateway in each Region, attach ...": A transit virtual interface is [attached to an AWS Direct Connect gateway](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-transit-vif-attaches-only-to-dxgw) and can reach both, but two transit gateways add attachments and route tables to run.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a second VPC in us-east-1" instead: a second private virtual interface to that VPC also works, because the VPC has [a virtual private gateway in the same Region](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-private-vif-without-dxgw-reaches-associated-region-only).

**Takeaway.** One Direct Connect connection reaches VPCs in several Regions through a Direct Connect gateway.

**Review.** [A Direct Connect connection is a port and its virtual interfaces choose the destination](2-deep.md#a-direct-connect-connection-is-a-port-and-its-virtual-interfaces-choose-the-destination-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=hybrid-networking-q004 -->
### Question 2

A company runs a mission-critical application in AWS that reads order data from its on-premises data center every minute. The data center connects to AWS through one AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection at one Direct Connect location. The connectivity must survive the failure of a device, a connection, or a whole Direct Connect location. Which design will make the connectivity the MOST resilient?

- Add three dedicated connections at the current location, and combine all four connections in a link aggregation group (LAG) for the traffic.
- Keep the current dedicated connection, and add a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet as the backup path for the traffic.
- Add a second dedicated connection at the current location, and make sure that it ends on a different AWS device from the first one.
- Add connections at a second Direct Connect location, so that each of the two locations has two connections that end on separate devices.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add connections at a second Direct Connect location, so that each of the two locations has two connections that end on separate devices.

**Deciding phrases.** "mission-critical application", "a whole Direct Connect location", "MOST resilient"

**Why.** The deciding phrase is the failure of a whole Direct Connect location. AWS recommends [making connections at multiple AWS Direct Connect locations](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-high-availability-multiple-locations), and the maximum resiliency model can reach [an SLA of 99.99%](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-resiliency-maximum-sla-99-99) when you meet the SLA requirements.

**Why not.**

- "Add three dedicated connections at the current location, ...": A LAG ends at one location, and it [will not protect against a single device failure](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-lag-not-more-resilient-against-device-failure) there or against the loss of that location.
- "Keep the current dedicated connection, and add a ...": A VPN backup avoids the location, but [performance over the internet is best effort](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-internet-vpn-best-effort-low-cost-widely-available), so it ranks below a second Direct Connect location.
- "Add a second dedicated connection at the current ...": Connections that [terminate on separate devices in one location](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-resiliency-dev-test-one-location-no-location-failure-protection) give no protection when that whole location fails.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a development workload that can stop when a location fails" instead: two connections at one location, because that model uses connections that [terminate on separate devices in one location](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-resiliency-dev-test-one-location-no-location-failure-protection).

**Takeaway.** The most resilient Direct Connect design uses two locations and separate devices, not a LAG at one location.

**Review.** [Direct Connect resilience comes from a second location and not from more links](2-deep.md#direct-connect-resilience-comes-from-a-second-location-and-not-from-more-links-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=hybrid-networking-q007 -->
### Question 3

A company has employees who work from home on laptops. The employees must reach internal applications that run on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets of a VPC in one AWS Region. They must sign in with the company's existing SAML 2.0 identity provider. The company wants a fully managed remote access solution. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection from each laptop to a virtual private gateway, with one customer gateway for each employee.
- Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint that uses federated authentication with the SAML 2.0 identity provider, and give users the AWS provided client.
- Run an OpenVPN server on an Amazon EC2 instance, connect it to the identity provider, and patch and scale the instance as users grow.
- Order an AWS Direct Connect hosted connection for each home office, and attach a private virtual interface to the VPC for each one.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint that uses federated authentication with the SAML 2.0 identity provider, and give users the AWS provided client.

**Deciding phrases.** "work from home on laptops", "SAML 2.0 identity provider", "fully managed", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The deciding phrases are employees on laptops and the SAML 2.0 identity provider. AWS says to consider Client VPN to [securely connect remote users to your VPCs](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-vs-site-to-site-decision-guide-remote-users), and Client VPN is [a managed client-based VPN service](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-definition-managed-client-based-vpn-openvpn).

**Why not.**

- "Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection from each laptop ...": Site-to-Site VPN is for connecting [an entire on-premises network](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-decision-guide-connect-entire-network-to-vpcs) to VPCs, not single laptops of remote employees.
- "Run an OpenVPN server on an Amazon EC2 ...": It works, but the team patches and scales the instance itself; Client VPN is [an AWS managed high availability and scalability service](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-whitepaper-managed-secure-software-remote-access).
- "Order an AWS Direct Connect hosted connection for ...": Direct Connect gives [dedicated, private network connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-bypasses-internet-dedicated-private) between a network and AWS, so a circuit to each home solves a problem the employees do not have.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a branch office network" instead: a Site-to-Site VPN connection, because it can connect [an entire on-premises network](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-decision-guide-connect-entire-network-to-vpcs) to VPCs.

**Takeaway.** People on laptops use Client VPN; whole networks use Site-to-Site VPN.

**Review.** [Choose it or not](1-fast.md#choose-it-or-not-2-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company must connect its on-premises data center to a VPC in one AWS Region. All traffic between the data center and the VPC must be encrypted in transit. The connection must be ready as soon as possible, within one week, and the traffic is low. The company has a router in the data center that supports IPsec. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet from the data center router to a virtual private gateway that is attached to the VPC.
- Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, and create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over it from the data center router to the VPC.
- Launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon EC2 instance in the VPC, and connect it to the data center router with IPsec over the internet.
- Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, and launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon EC2 instance that ends IPsec over the connection.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet from the data center router to a virtual private gateway that is attached to the VPC.

**Deciding phrases.** "as soon as possible, within one week", "the traffic is low", "encrypted in transit", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The deciding phrases are the one-week deadline and the low traffic. A Site-to-Site VPN gives [Internet Protocol security (IPsec) VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-definition-ipsec-vpc-to-on-premises) between the data center and the VPC, and it [can be configured in minutes](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vpn-ipsec-over-internet-quick-low-bandwidth). A new Direct Connect dedicated connection takes [from several weeks to a few months](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-time-dedicated-weeks-to-months), with or without a VPN on top.

**Why not.**

- "Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, ...": A new dedicated connection can take [from several weeks to a few months](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-time-dedicated-weeks-to-months) to install, so it misses the one-week deadline.
- "Launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon ...": It works, but [you must manage the software appliance](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-software-vpn-ec2-you-manage-appliance-single-point-of-failure), including its patches, which is more work than a Site-to-Site VPN connection.
- "Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, ...": The new dedicated connection takes [from several weeks to a few months](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-time-dedicated-weeks-to-months), so the design fails the deadline before the appliance adds its own work.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The company needs consistent network performance for large, steady transfers, and the connection can be ready in four months" instead: a VPN over Direct Connect, for [more consistent performance than the internet can provide](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-decision-guide-more-consistent-performance-than-internet).

**Takeaway.** A deadline of days and low traffic point to a Site-to-Site VPN, not a new Direct Connect port.

**Review.** [Choose it or not](1-fast.md#choose-it-or-not-2-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=hybrid-networking-q005 -->
### Question 5

A company must connect its on-premises data center to a VPC in one AWS Region. All traffic between the data center and the VPC must be encrypted in transit. The company needs consistent network performance for large, steady transfers, and the connection can be ready in four months. The company has a router in the data center that supports IPsec. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet from the data center router to a virtual private gateway that is attached to the VPC.
- Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, and create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over it from the data center router to the VPC.
- Launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon EC2 instance in the VPC, and connect it to the data center router with IPsec over the internet.
- Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, and launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon EC2 instance that ends IPsec over the connection.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, and create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over it from the data center router to the VPC.

**Deciding phrases.** "consistent network performance", "large, steady transfers", "encrypted in transit", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The deciding phrase is consistent network performance for large, steady transfers. Direct Connect fits it, but it [does not encrypt your traffic](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-not-encrypted-by-default-use-service-encryption) by default. To encrypt, you [establish a VPN over Direct Connect](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-encrypt-private-connection-vpn-over-dx-or-macsec), which needs no instance to run.

**Why not.**

- "Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet ...": The VPN is quick to create, but [performance over the internet is best effort](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-internet-vpn-best-effort-low-cost-widely-available), so it does not give consistent performance.
- "Launch a software VPN appliance on an Amazon ...": The appliance still sends IPsec across the internet, where [performance over the internet is best effort](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-internet-vpn-best-effort-low-cost-widely-available), and the team also patches it.
- "Order a new AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection, ...": It works, but [you must manage the software appliance](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-software-vpn-ec2-you-manage-appliance-single-point-of-failure); a Site-to-Site VPN over the same connection encrypts without an instance to run.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The connection must be ready as soon as possible, within one week, and the traffic is low" instead: a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet, because it [can be configured in minutes](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vpn-ipsec-over-internet-quick-low-bandwidth).

**Takeaway.** Consistent performance points to Direct Connect, and a Site-to-Site VPN over it adds IPsec encryption.

**Review.** [Choose it or not](1-fast.md#choose-it-or-not-2-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=hybrid-networking-q008 -->
### Question 6

A company sends traffic from its data center to a VPC over a private line: an AWS Direct Connect connection with a private virtual interface. A new security rule says that all traffic on this connection must be encrypted in transit. The connection is a 10 Gbps dedicated connection, the router and location support MACsec, and the encryption must not reduce the MTU. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on MACsec for the Direct Connect connection, and configure the matching MACsec keys on the company router at the Direct Connect location.
- Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection that runs IPsec over the Direct Connect connection, and route the VPC traffic through the VPN tunnels.
- Keep the current design, because traffic on a Direct Connect connection stays off the internet and is encrypted on the private line.
- Turn on TLS encryption in every application that sends data between the data center and the VPC, and keep the virtual interface unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on MACsec for the Direct Connect connection, and configure the matching MACsec keys on the company router at the Direct Connect location.

**Deciding phrases.** "10 Gbps dedicated connection", "the router and location support MACsec", "must not reduce the MTU", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The deciding phrases are the 10 Gbps dedicated connection and the MTU. MACsec is supported on [10 Gbps, 100 Gbps, and 400 Gbps dedicated AWS Direct Connect connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-macsec-supported-dedicated-10-100-400-gbps), and [you will need a MACsec-capable device](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-macsec-needs-capable-device), which the company router is. A VPN would also encrypt, but [it reduces the MTU size](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vpn-over-dx-adds-encryption-reduces-mtu).

**Why not.**

- "Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection that runs IPsec ...": A VPN over Direct Connect adds encryption, but [it reduces the MTU size](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vpn-over-dx-adds-encryption-reduces-mtu), so it breaks the MTU requirement.
- "Keep the current design, because traffic on a ...": Direct Connect [does not encrypt your traffic](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-not-encrypted-by-default-use-service-encryption) in transit by default, so the private line alone breaks the new security rule.
- "Turn on TLS encryption in every application that ...": It works, because you can [use the transit encryption options for that service](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-not-encrypted-by-default-use-service-encryption), but changing every application is more work than MACsec on one link.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The connection is a 1 Gbps hosted connection from a Direct Connect Partner" instead: an IPsec VPN over Direct Connect, because MACsec does not run on [any hosted connections](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-macsec-not-on-1gbps-or-hosted).

**Takeaway.** When the router and the location support MACsec, MACsec encrypts the link without the MTU cost of an IPsec VPN.

**Review.** [Direct Connect traffic is private but not encrypted unless you add encryption](2-deep.md#direct-connect-traffic-is-private-but-not-encrypted-unless-you-add-encryption-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company connects its data center to one VPC with two Site-to-Site VPN connections to a virtual private gateway. The connections use static routing. Nightly transfers now need several times the bandwidth of one VPN tunnel, and the design must be scalable as the transfers grow. The company does not want to use AWS Direct Connect yet. The customer gateway devices support BGP. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Attach the VPN connections to a transit gateway instead of the virtual private gateway, and turn on equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) routing support on it.
- Add three more Site-to-Site VPN connections to the existing virtual private gateway, and spread the data center prefixes across all of the tunnels.
- Turn on acceleration for the existing VPN connections, so that the tunnels use the AWS global network and carry more traffic each night.
- Use dynamic routing with BGP for the VPN connections, and advertise the data center prefixes from the customer gateway devices on every tunnel.
- Replace the virtual private gateway with software VPN appliances on Amazon EC2 instances, and split the tunnels across the instances with custom routing scripts.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Attach the VPN connections to a transit gateway instead of the virtual private gateway, and turn on equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) routing support on it.
- Use dynamic routing with BGP for the VPN connections, and advertise the data center prefixes from the customer gateway devices on every tunnel.

**Deciding phrases.** "several times the bandwidth of one VPN tunnel", "use static routing", "The customer gateway devices support BGP", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The deciding phrase is several times the bandwidth of one tunnel. A transit gateway spreads traffic across many tunnels with ECMP, and the connections [must be configured for dynamic routing](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-needs-dynamic-routing-not-static). On a virtual private gateway, [ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-not-on-vgw-supported-on-tgw).

- On a virtual private gateway [ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-not-on-vgw-supported-on-tgw); for higher throughput the VPN FAQ says to [use AWS Transit Gateway](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-faq-tgw-for-higher-throughput).
- For ECMP the VPN connections [must be configured for dynamic routing](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-needs-dynamic-routing-not-static), because [ECMP is not supported using static routing](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-tgw-vpn-ecmp-requires-dynamic-routing-whitepaper).

**Why not.**

- "Add three more Site-to-Site VPN connections to the ...": On a virtual private gateway [ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-not-on-vgw-supported-on-tgw), so the gateway uses one tunnel and more connections add no bandwidth.
- "Turn on acceleration for the existing VPN connections, ...": [You cannot turn on or turn off acceleration](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-accelerated-cannot-toggle-on-existing) on an existing connection, and virtual private gateways [do not support accelerated VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-accelerated-transit-gateway-only).
- "Replace the virtual private gateway with software VPN ...": Appliances can spread the load, but [you must manage the software appliance](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-software-vpn-ec2-you-manage-appliance-single-point-of-failure) and its scripts, which is more work than a transit gateway.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The customer gateway devices do not support BGP" instead: new devices come first, because [ECMP is not supported using static routing](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-tgw-vpn-ecmp-requires-dynamic-routing-whitepaper).

**Takeaway.** More VPN bandwidth than one tunnel comes from a transit gateway with ECMP and BGP, not from more connections on a virtual private gateway.

**Review.** [Each VPN tunnel has a bandwidth limit and a transit gateway combines tunnels](2-deep.md#each-vpn-tunnel-has-a-bandwidth-limit-and-a-transit-gateway-combines-tunnels-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company uses a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection as the primary path from its data center to a virtual private gateway. A Site-to-Site VPN connection to the same virtual private gateway is the backup path for this mission-critical traffic. However, in a failover test, the VPN cannot carry the load. The company needs a highly available design in which the backup path carries the full load when the primary connection fails. Which solution will provide the HIGHEST availability?

- Use AS path prepending on the Direct Connect routes, so that the VPN connection carries part of the traffic at all times.
- Add three more Site-to-Site VPN connections to the same virtual private gateway, so that the backup tunnels can share the full load.
- Order a second 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection at a second Direct Connect location, and use it as the backup path for the traffic.
- Order a second 10 Gbps connection at the same Direct Connect location, and add both connections to one link aggregation group (LAG).

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Order a second 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection at a second Direct Connect location, and use it as the backup path for the traffic.

**Deciding phrases.** "10 Gbps", "the VPN cannot carry the load", "carries the full load", "HIGHEST availability"

**Why.** The deciding phrase is the full load of a 10 Gbps connection. A VPN on a virtual private gateway gives [up to 1.25 Gbps throughput per VPN tunnel](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-backup-vpn-bandwidth-limit-not-above-1-gbps), and teams that ignore this [overestimate their backup capabilities](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-wa-anti-pattern-overestimating-vpn-backup-bandwidth). A second Direct Connect connection at another location carries the same load.

**Why not.**

- "Use AS path prepending on the Direct Connect ...": The Direct Connect path wins [regardless of AS path prepending](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vpn-same-vpc-failover-only-dx-path-preferred), so the VPN carries traffic only after a failure.
- "Add three more Site-to-Site VPN connections to the ...": On a virtual private gateway [ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-ecmp-not-on-vgw-supported-on-tgw), so one tunnel of [up to 1.25 Gbps](../facts/site-to-site-vpn.md#site-to-site-vpn-limit-bandwidth-standard-tunnel) carries the backup, far below the 10 Gbps load.
- "Order a second 10 Gbps connection at the ...": It carries the load after one link fails, but a LAG [will not protect against a single device failure](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-lag-not-more-resilient-against-device-failure) where it ends.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a non-critical workload on a 1 Gbps connection" instead: a VPN backup is a fair choice, because one tunnel gives [up to 1.25 Gbps throughput per VPN tunnel](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-backup-vpn-bandwidth-limit-not-above-1-gbps).

**Takeaway.** Back up a fast Direct Connect connection with another Direct Connect connection at a second location.

**Review.** [Direct Connect resilience comes from a second location and not from more links](2-deep.md#direct-connect-resilience-comes-from-a-second-location-and-not-from-more-links-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=hybrid-networking-q010 -->
### Question 9

A company runs an analytics workload in a VPC. The company needs a private line from its data center to the VPC that does not use the internet. A capacity of 200 Mbps is sufficient for the next three years. The company has no network equipment in a Direct Connect location and does not want to place any there. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Request a 200 Mbps dedicated connection in the Direct Connect console, and order a cross-connect at the Direct Connect location.
- Request a 10 Gbps dedicated connection, and work with a partner to extend the data center network to the Direct Connect location.
- Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet to a virtual private gateway, and size the customer gateway device for 200 Mbps.
- Ask an AWS Direct Connect Partner for a 200 Mbps hosted connection, and create a private virtual interface on it to the VPC.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Ask an AWS Direct Connect Partner for a 200 Mbps hosted connection, and create a private virtual interface on it to the VPC.

**Deciding phrases.** "does not use the internet", "200 Mbps is sufficient", "no network equipment in a Direct Connect location", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The deciding phrases are 200 Mbps and no equipment in a Direct Connect location. Partners [can help you extend your preexisting data center](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-partners-extend-network-to-location) to a Direct Connect location. A partner [provisions on behalf of a customer](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-hosted-connection-provisioned-by-partner) a hosted connection of the size the company orders, so the company pays for no unused port capacity.

**Why not.**

- "Request a 200 Mbps dedicated connection in the ...": A dedicated connection has a port speed of [1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, 100 Gbps, and 400 Gbps](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-limit-dedicated-port-speeds), so 200 Mbps is not a dedicated speed.
- "Request a 10 Gbps dedicated connection, and work ...": It works, but port hours are charged even when [no data is passing through the port](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-port-hours-charged-even-when-no-data), so the larger port costs more for capacity that the company does not use.
- "Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection over the internet ...": It costs less, but the stem rules out the internet, and a Site-to-Site VPN runs [over the public internet](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-faq-vpn-ipsec-over-internet-quick-low-bandwidth).

**Twin.** If the stem said "The connection can use the internet" instead: a Site-to-Site VPN, because it has [low cost and is widely available](../facts/direct-connect.md#direct-connect-vs-vpn-internet-vpn-best-effort-low-cost-widely-available).

**Takeaway.** For a small capacity and no equipment at a location, ask a partner for a hosted connection.

**Review.** [A Direct Connect connection is a port and its virtual interfaces choose the destination](2-deep.md#a-direct-connect-connection-is-a-port-and-its-virtual-interfaces-choose-the-destination-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=hybrid-networking-q012 -->
### Question 10

A company has an AWS Client VPN endpoint that is associated with a subnet of a VPC, and remote users reach resources in that VPC. The VPC reaches an on-premises network, 172.16.0.0/16, through a Site-to-Site VPN connection, and its route tables and security groups already allow traffic from the client CIDR range. Users must also reach the on-premises network through Client VPN. The company wants to restrict the tunnel to traffic for the VPC and the on-premises network. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Change the client CIDR range of the endpoint to 172.16.0.0/22, so that clients get addresses inside the on-premises network range.
- Add a route to 172.16.0.0/16 through the associated subnet in the endpoint route table, and add an authorization rule for 172.16.0.0/16.
- Add an authorization rule that denies access to 0.0.0.0/0, so that internet traffic from the clients cannot use the tunnel.
- Create a new Client VPN endpoint with split-tunnel turned on, copy the routes and rules to it, and move every user to the new endpoint.
- Turn on split-tunnel on the existing endpoint, so that only traffic that matches a route in the endpoint route table uses the tunnel.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Add a route to 172.16.0.0/16 through the associated subnet in the endpoint route table, and add an authorization rule for 172.16.0.0/16.
- Turn on split-tunnel on the existing endpoint, so that only traffic that matches a route in the endpoint route table uses the tunnel.

**Deciding phrases.** "must also reach the on-premises network", "restrict the tunnel to traffic for the VPC and the on-premises network", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Two gaps exist. A network outside the VPC needs a route and an authorization rule on the endpoint. With split-tunnel on, [only traffic with a destination to the network](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-default-off-all-traffic-through-tunnel) of a route goes over the tunnel, so internet traffic stays on the local network.

- To reach another network, you [add a route to the specific network](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-other-networks-need-route-and-authorization-rule) in the endpoint route table and [add authorization rule enabling access](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-other-networks-need-route-and-authorization-rule) to it.
- By default [all traffic from clients is routed](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-default-off-all-traffic-through-tunnel) over the tunnel; with split-tunnel on, [only traffic with a destination to the network](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-default-off-all-traffic-through-tunnel) of a route uses it.

**Why not.**

- "Change the client CIDR range of the endpoint ...": [The client CIDR range cannot be changed](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-client-cidr-cannot-change-after-creation) after you create the endpoint, and clients need a route, not on-premises addresses.
- "Add an authorization rule that denies access to ...": [The default behavior is to deny access](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-authorization-rules-default-deny-no-restrict-rules), and you [cannot add an authorization rule to restrict access](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-authorization-rules-default-deny-no-restrict-rules) to a network.
- "Create a new Client VPN endpoint with split-tunnel ...": It works, because split-tunnel can be turned on [on a new or existing Client VPN endpoint](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-disabled-by-default-at-creation), but a new endpoint and new user profiles are more work.

**Twin.** If the stem said "all user traffic, including internet traffic, must go through the tunnel" instead: keep split-tunnel off, because then [all traffic from clients is routed](../facts/client-vpn.md#client-vpn-split-tunnel-default-off-all-traffic-through-tunnel) through it.

**Takeaway.** Client VPN reaches another network through a route plus an authorization rule; split-tunnel limits what uses the tunnel.

**Review.** [Client VPN connects people to a VPC through an endpoint in a subnet](2-deep.md#client-vpn-connects-people-to-a-vpc-through-an-endpoint-in-a-subnet-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
